html:
A church in Rome, a short walk east of the Colosseum, dedicated to Pope Clement I, one of the first bishops of Rome. It is three layers on one site. The church at street level was built in one campaign by Cardinal Anastasius from about 1099 to about 1120. Under it lies a 4th-century church, and under that the Roman buildings the first church replaced.

The lowest level holds the foundations of a building probably destroyed in the Great Fire of 64, then a large industrial building, probably the imperial mint, and an apartment block across a narrow alley. About 200 a shrine of Mithras was built in the block's courtyard: a low vaulted room about 9.6 m by 6 m, made to look like a cave, with an altar carved with Mithras killing the bull. In the 4th century the lower floors were filled with rubble and a church built over them; Jerome wrote of it in 392. Its walls carry the largest group of early medieval paintings in Rome after Santa Maria Antiqua. One 11th-century fresco of a miracle of Saint Clement has words painted beside it in the spoken Italian of the day, a pagan cursing his servants, among the earliest written lines of the language.

An old story said the lower church burned in the Norman sack of 1084 under Robert Guiscard, but no trace of fire has been found, and why it was filled in and built over is still debated. The upper church has three naves on ancient columns, an inlaid Cosmatesque floor, a 12th-century choir enclosure made partly from marble of the older church, and an apse mosaic of the Triumph of the Cross, one of the finest Roman mosaics of its century. Irish Dominicans have held it since 1667, and their prior Joseph Mullooly found the lower church in the 1860s; the Mithras shrine, found in 1867, could only be explored in 1914, once it was drained. A side chapel holds the tomb of Saint Cyril, who with his brother Methodius took Christianity to the Slavs and made the Glagolitic alphabet.
